summary:
SPEX is a web app for exploring NASA's SPHEREx infrared sky images taken at different times.
It measures how objects appear to move, using Gaia stars as a reference, reports the uncertainty, and adds an AI guide, a course and a game.
details:
SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colors, from 0.75 to 5 micrometers, and comes back to each part of the sky about every six months. That means moving objects can be spotted by comparing the images. The data comes as FITS files, which are hard to open without special software. We built SPEX so a student can just look at the images, and so someone who wants the numbers can get those too.

What it does You pick a target or type in sky coordinates. SPEX downloads real SPHEREx cutouts from NASA/IPAC IRSA and lines up the observations from different survey passes. You can blink between them, play them as a sequence, see motion trails, and open spectra, light curves and a difference image. Every measurement shows its uncertainty. When a result is too weak to trust, the app says so.

How it works

Getting the data. Our Express backend queries IRSA's TAP service (the spherex.plane and spherex.artifact tables), keeps the newest release for each observation (DR1, then QR3, then QR2) and downloads FITS cutouts. Downloads are cached on the server, with a 256 MiB limit.
Reading the files. We wrote our own FITS reader and WCS code. It handles TAN-SIP distortion and the WCS-WAVE table that gives a wavelength for each pixel, and it reads the flux, variance, quality flag and ePSF extensions.
Time. Exposures are grouped into survey passes, so the gaps you see between frames are the real ones, about six months. We never resample or fill in time.
Astrometry. Each frame is compared with isolated Gaia DR3 stars. We use a sigma-clipped shift, or an affine fit when six or more stars are available. Saturated and non-functional pixels are masked. Position and proper motion come from a weighted linear fit over time, with weights of 1/sigma squared. We run the fit twice: once with unsaturated frames only, and once with PSF-wing fits included, which we always mark as low confidence. Each detector also gets an error floor, added in quadrature.
Significance. Motion counts as detected only if the displacement is at least 3 sigma of the target's own error and it agrees with the expected motion within 2 sigma.
Mr. SPEX, the AI guide. When a user clicks a pixel, the server works out its sky coordinates, the nearby Gaia and AllWISE sources, the local flux and signal-to-noise, any data-quality warnings and verified facts about the target. Gemini then explains that spot in plain language. Without an API key, the app shows a template explanation built from the same measured data.
Learning and community. There is an Academy with 6 levels (lessons, SVG diagrams, practice questions, exams), Explorer missions, a 6-chapter story game called Cosmic Detective with mini-games and a 3D station built in Three.js, XP and ranks, and a community page for discovery notes, reports and bad-data flags. The interface works in English and Arabic (right-to-left).

Checking it on known objects We ran the pipeline on five targets whose behavior is already known. This tests the method. We are not claiming any discovery.

Barnard's Star: 4.00 sigma, motion detected, 0.48 sigma from the expected value.
Epsilon Indi B: 3.26 sigma, motion detected, 0.27 sigma from the expected value.
WISE 0855-0714: 1.39 sigma, reported as not significant.
RW Aurigae and R Draconis (both should not move): 0.47 and 0.38 sigma, so not significant, as expected.

Limitations The time baselines are short, about 370 to 520 days. Pixels are 6.2 arcseconds across. Bright stars saturate, so for those we rely on PSF-wing fits and mark the result low confidence.

If the archive takes more than about 12 seconds to answer, the app switches to saved snapshots and shows "Showing saved snapshot". The game uses synthetic data, labelled as such and kept apart from the real pipeline.

Research paper Alongside the app, we wrote a full research paper that explains how the engine works and the math behind it: the astrometry, the error budget and the significance test. It is a PDF you can read here
